analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 34 House sponsors but never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and died in committee when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have deleted the 'non-interference' rule that bars the federal government from negotiating drug prices under Medicare Part D. Instead, the Secretary of Health and Human Services would have had to bargain with pharmaceutical manufacturers over the prices, discounts, and rebates charged for drugs used by people in Medicare drug plans, starting in 2016, and report to Congress twice a year on the savings achieved. The bill was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million Medicare beneficiaries who get drug coverage through Part D plans and Medicare Advantage would benefit if the government could negotiate lower prices, through lower out-of-pocket drug costs and reduced pressure on Medicare premiums and taxpayer spending.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the statutory 'noninterference' provision in Medicare Part D law and directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices, discounts, rebates, and other price concessions with pharmaceutical manufacturers for covered Part D drugs [S2][S3].

Negotiated lower prices would apply to what manufacturers charge Medicare drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans, and plan sponsors would remain free to negotiate even deeper discounts below the negotiated price [S3].
The Secretary would have to report to Congress every six months on the negotiations and the price discounts actually achieved, creating public accountability for the savings [S3].
The bill preserves the existing rules on plan formularies, meaning beneficiaries' access requirements under current law would not be changed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost, as negotiated prices, rebates, and discounts would reduce the revenue they currently receive from Medicare Part D. Opponents also argued that lower revenues could reduce investment in developing new drugs.

drawbacks.text: Without authority to establish or require a particular formulary, the Secretary's negotiating leverage is limited; price negotiation alone, without credible exclusion of drugs from coverage, may achieve smaller savings than supporters hoped [S3].

Opponents of Medicare price negotiation have long argued that cutting drug revenues would reduce manufacturers' returns and could slow the development of new medicines; the bill contains no offsetting mechanism for innovation concerns (general policy objection, not from the provided sources).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: Medicare is one of the largest drug buyers in the world, and the current law expressly forbids it from negotiating, so beneficiaries and taxpayers pay more than they might otherwise. The main design weakness is that negotiation without formulary authority is a blunt tool, so the actual savings could fall short of expectations. The main trade-off acknowledged by opponents is possible reduced investment in new drug development. On balance the bill would shift billions in bargaining power from drug makers to Medicare beneficiaries, with uncertain but likely positive savings for consumers and taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and their health subcommittees, and neither committee ever held a hearing or voted on it, so the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the Medicare Prescription Drug Price Negotiation Act on July 14, 2015, with six original cosponsors including Rep. Jan Schakowsky and Rep. Louise Slaughter [S1][S3].
The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the two panels with jurisdiction over Medicare and health policy [S1][S5].
Within a week, it was referred to the health subcommittees of both committees, where the record ends; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded [S5].
A total of 33 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, and all sponsorship was Democratic [S4].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without the bill ever advancing out of committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: the 'noninterference' provision barring Medicare price negotiation remained in force, and Part D plans continued paying manufacturer-set prices. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require the HHS Secretary to negotiate Medicare Part D drug prices.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, supporting Medicare drug price negotiation.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 33 cosponsors were House Democrats, though the bill's introduction included a Republican original cosponsor, Rep. Louise Slaughter; no votes were ever taken, and the committees that buried it were chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would replace the current system, in which the law bars Medicare from negotiating, with mandatory government negotiation of prices, rebates, and discounts, cutting manufacturer revenue from the largest public drug program. Their interest in keeping the non-interference rule runs directly against beneficiaries' pocketbooks.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plan sponsors
industries.note: Negotiation would still flow through private Part D plans and their pharmacy benefit intermediaries, and the bill expressly lets plans seek discounts below the negotiated price, keeping their middleman role intact while they benefit from lower input prices.
